title: Model Routing & Fallback
summary: Not every request deserves the biggest model. Routing sends easy, high-volume calls to a cheap, fast model and hard ones to a frontier model, using a classifier or cheap heuristic to decide. Fallback is the safety net: when a model errors, times out, or refuses, you retry down an ordered chain of alternatives so a single provider hiccup never becomes a user-facing failure. Together they cut cost and latency while raising reliability.

subtopics.title: Why route: most requests don't need the frontier model
subtopics.explanation: In real traffic, a large share of requests are simple — classification, extraction, short lookups — that a small model answers just as well for a fraction of the cost and latency. Sending everything to the frontier model overpays on the easy majority and slows every response. Routing exists to spend your expensive capacity only where the task's difficulty actually demands it.
subtopics.example:
# without routing: every call pays frontier price and latency
answer = frontier_model.generate(prompt)

# with routing: match model to task difficulty
if is_simple(prompt):
    answer = small_model.generate(prompt)   # cheap + fast
else:
    answer = frontier_model.generate(prompt)  # only when needed
# the easy majority no longer subsidizes the hard minority

subtopics.title: Deciding which model: heuristic or cheap classifier
subtopics.explanation: The router needs a fast, cheap decision so it doesn't add its own latency: a rule (input length, presence of code, required tools) or a small classifier model that labels the request's difficulty. The decision must be far cheaper than the call it's routing, or the router costs more than it saves. A good routing signal is the whole game — it determines how much you save without hurting quality.

subtopics.title: The fallback chain: try alternatives in order
subtopics.explanation: A fallback chain is an ordered list of models you attempt in sequence: if the first fails, you move to the next, and so on, until one succeeds or the chain is exhausted. Each attempt is wrapped so a failure is caught and turns into 'try the next one' rather than an exception to the user. The chain is what converts a single point of failure into a degraded-but-working path.

subtopics.title: Fall back on the right signals: timeouts and error classes
subtopics.explanation: Not every failure should trigger a fallback: a timeout, a 5xx, or a rate-limit is transient and worth retrying elsewhere, but a malformed-request (4xx) or a content-policy refusal will fail the same way on every model. You classify the error and only fall back on the recoverable kinds, ideally after a bounded timeout so a hung call doesn't stall the chain. Distinguishing retryable from terminal errors is what keeps fallback from wasting calls on hopeless requests.

subtopics.title: Measure and tune: cost, quality, and escalation rate
subtopics.explanation: A router is only as good as its metrics: you track the fraction sent to each tier, the quality on routed-cheap requests, and how often you escalate or fall back. If cheap-tier quality drops, you tighten the heuristic; if fallbacks spike, a provider is degraded. Continuously measuring routing decisions is what lets you push more traffic to the cheap tier safely instead of guessing.

foundations.overview: Model routing and fallback are two complementary patterns that sit in front of your model calls. Routing is a proactive cost-and-latency optimization: a cheap, fast decision — a heuristic on the request or a small classifier — chooses the smallest model capable of the task, so the easy majority of traffic goes to a small/fast model and only genuinely hard requests reach the frontier model. The decision itself must be far cheaper than the call it governs, or the router erases its own savings. Fallback is a reactive reliability pattern: instead of a single model call that can fail, you define an ordered chain of alternatives and try them in sequence, catching each failure and moving to the next until one succeeds or the chain is exhausted. The subtlety is deciding what counts as a failure worth falling back on — transient errors (timeouts, 429 rate limits, 5xx) are worth retrying on another model, while terminal errors (malformed requests, policy refusals) will fail identically everywhere and should short-circuit. A bounded per-attempt timeout keeps one hung call from stalling the whole chain. In practice the two combine: routing picks a starting tier, and each tier has its own fallback chain. The pattern is governed by metrics — the share of traffic per tier, cheap-tier quality, and escalation/fallback rates — which tell you when it's safe to push more traffic downtier and when a provider is degrading.
foundations.formalDefinition: Model routing is the selection of which model handles a request based on a cheap difficulty signal computed before the call; fallback is an ordered retry policy that, on a retryable failure, attempts the next model in a predefined chain until one succeeds or the chain is exhausted, distinguishing retryable (transient) from terminal (deterministic) errors.
foundations.whyItMatters: Routing directly reduces cost and latency by not overspending frontier capacity on easy requests, often the largest lever at scale; fallback converts single-provider failures — outages, rate limits, timeouts — into a degraded-but-working path, which is essential for an agent that must stay up under real traffic.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a support desk. Routing is triage: the receptionist sends routine questions to a fast junior agent and only escalates the genuinely hard cases to the senior specialist, so you don't pay specialist rates for password resets. Fallback is the escalation ladder for when someone is unavailable: if the first agent is out (timeout) or overloaded (rate limit) you route to the next available agent, but if the request is simply invalid you don't keep passing it around — it fails the same way for everyone.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Cost-optimized assistants sending classification and formatting to small models and complex reasoning to frontier models, multi-provider setups that fail over between vendors during an outage, and agent gateways that combine a routing tier with per-tier fallback chains and bounded timeouts.
commonUseCases: Routing high-volume easy requests to a cheap/fast model
Failing over to a secondary model/provider on timeout or 5xx
Escalating a low-confidence cheap-model answer to the frontier model
Multi-provider redundancy to survive a single vendor outage

commonMisconceptions.myth: The router should use a big model to decide routing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The routing decision must be far cheaper than the call it routes — a heuristic or tiny classifier. Using an expensive model to choose defeats the point by adding cost and latency up front.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Fallback should retry on every error.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only transient errors (timeouts, 429, 5xx) are worth falling back on. A malformed request or policy refusal fails identically on every model, so retrying it down the chain just wastes calls and time.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Falling back to another model is free reliability.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fallback models may be slower, pricier, or lower quality, and an unbounded chain adds latency. You bound attempts, set per-attempt timeouts, and treat an exhausted chain as a handled failure.

interactiveExamples.title: A difficulty router plus a fallback chain
interactiveExamples.explanation: A cheap heuristic picks a starting tier, and each attempt is wrapped so a retryable failure moves to the next model in the chain. The fake models simulate a primary that times out, so the call falls back to the secondary.

code.caption: The easy tier tries 'small' first and succeeds; had it failed, the chain would escalate to 'frontier'.
code.expectedOutput:
tier: easy
[small] answered: classify this ticket

interactiveExamples.title: Retryable vs terminal errors in the chain
interactiveExamples.explanation: Fallback should only fire on transient errors. Here a terminal BadRequest short-circuits the whole chain, while a transient RateLimit falls through to the next model — so hopeless requests fail fast instead of wasting every model.

code.caption: The rate-limited call escalates to the secondary; the malformed request fails immediately without wasting the chain.
code.expectedOutput:
[secondary] ok
terminal, not retried: invalid input

checkpoints.prompt: What must be true of the routing decision itself?
options: It should use the frontier model for accuracy
It must be far cheaper and faster than the call it routes
It must always pick the largest model
It should be made after the model responds
checkpoints.explanation: A router adds a decision before every call, so the decision (a heuristic or tiny classifier) must cost far less than the call it governs — otherwise it erases the savings it was meant to create.

checkpoints.prompt: This fallback chain retries on any exception. Why is that a problem?
options: It should use a while loop
It retries terminal errors (e.g. malformed request, policy refusal) that fail identically on every model, wasting the whole chain
call_model needs a timeout argument name
checkpoints.explanation: Catching every Exception means a deterministic failure (bad request, content refusal) is retried on every model even though it will fail the same way each time. Fall back only on retryable/transient errors; let terminal errors short-circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: Given choose_tier returns 'easy' for short prompts, what tier prints?
checkpoints.explanation: The prompt is short (well under 200 chars) and no tools are needed, so neither condition triggers and the router defaults the easy majority to the 'easy' tier.

theory.question: How does model routing reduce cost and latency without hurting quality?
theory.directAnswer: Routing uses a cheap difficulty signal to send the easy majority of requests to a small, fast model and reserve the frontier model for genuinely hard tasks, so you stop overpaying frontier price and latency on requests a small model handles equally well. Quality is protected by measuring cheap-tier accuracy and escalating (or falling back) when the signal indicates difficulty or the cheap answer is low-confidence.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A dispatch layer that picks which model handles a request based on a fast, inexpensive decision made before the call.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real traffic is dominated by simple requests; sending them all to the frontier model wastes cost and adds latency the task doesn't require.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A heuristic (length, tools needed, keywords) or a tiny classifier labels the request's difficulty, selects a tier, and routes accordingly, with metrics on per-tier volume and quality to tune the threshold safely.

theory.whyImportant: At scale, routing is often the single largest cost lever, and because output-token generation is faster on smaller models it also improves latency for the majority of traffic.
theory.realWorldExample: An assistant routes ticket classification and short summaries to a small model and multi-step reasoning to the frontier model, cutting spend sharply while keeping quality steady on the hard cases.

followUps.question: What if the cheap model gets a hard request wrong?
followUps.answer: You add a confidence check or escalation rule so low-confidence cheap answers are re-run on the frontier model, and you tighten the routing heuristic based on observed errors.

followUps.question: Why not just use the small model for everything?
followUps.answer: Small models underperform on hard reasoning; routing keeps quality on the difficult minority while capturing savings on the easy majority.

theory.question: How do you design a fallback chain, and which failures should trigger a fallback?
theory.directAnswer: Define an ordered list of models and try them in sequence, catching failures and moving to the next until one succeeds or the chain is exhausted, wrapping each attempt in a bounded timeout. Fall back only on transient errors — timeouts, 429 rate limits, 5xx — and short-circuit terminal errors like malformed requests or policy refusals, because those fail identically on every model.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An ordered retry policy across alternative models that converts a single point of failure into a degraded-but-working path.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Any single model or provider can time out, rate-limit, or have an outage; without a fallback, that becomes a user-facing failure.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You classify the caught error as retryable or terminal, on retryable move to the next model in the chain (with a per-attempt timeout so a hung call doesn't stall it), and on an exhausted chain raise a single handled failure the caller can route to a default or human.

theory.whyImportant: It keeps an agent available under real-world provider instability, turning outages and rate limits into transparent failovers instead of downtime.
theory.realWorldExample: During a provider outage, calls that timed out on the primary model automatically failed over to a secondary provider, so users saw slightly slower answers instead of errors.

followUps.question: Why bound the chain and set timeouts?
followUps.answer: An unbounded chain or a hung call adds unbounded latency; bounding attempts and per-attempt timeouts keep worst-case response time predictable.

followUps.question: How do routing and fallback combine?
followUps.answer: Routing picks a starting tier and each tier has its own fallback chain, so you get both cost optimization and resilience in one gateway.

scenario.question: Your agent's costs tripled after moving all traffic to the frontier model for quality, but latency and spend are now unacceptable. Users still need high quality on the hard cases. How do you redesign the model layer?
scenario.directAnswer: Introduce a routing tier with a cheap difficulty signal so the easy majority goes to a small/fast model and only hard requests reach the frontier model, and add a per-tier fallback chain for resilience. Then measure cheap-tier quality and escalation rate, tightening the heuristic and adding a confidence-based escalation so hard cases still get frontier quality while the bulk of spend drops.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cost-quality rebalancing problem solved by adding routing plus fallback rather than a single flat model choice.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Sending all traffic to the frontier model overpays on the simple majority and inflates latency, but naively downgrading everything would hurt the hard cases.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Profile the traffic to find the easy-vs-hard split, build a heuristic/classifier router, route accordingly, add confidence-based escalation for borderline cheap answers, and instrument per-tier volume, quality, and fallback rate to tune safely.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the metrics-driven way to recover cost and latency without sacrificing quality where it matters, the core value of routing plus fallback in production.
scenario.realWorldExample: After profiling showed 70% of requests were classification and short summaries, routing them to a small model cut cost by more than half while a confidence escalation preserved frontier quality on the reasoning-heavy 30%.

followUps.question: How do you validate the router didn't hurt quality?
followUps.answer: Sample routed-cheap outputs against frontier answers offline and track a quality metric per tier, tightening the threshold if cheap-tier quality dips.

followUps.question: What guards against a provider outage in this design?
followUps.answer: Each tier's fallback chain fails over to a secondary model/provider on transient errors, so cost optimization and resilience coexist.

keyTakeaways: Routing sends the easy majority to a small/fast model and reserves the frontier model for hard requests, cutting cost and latency.
The routing decision (heuristic or tiny classifier) must be far cheaper than the call it governs, or it erases its own savings.
A fallback chain tries models in order, converting a single-provider failure into a degraded-but-working path.
Fall back only on transient errors (timeouts, 429, 5xx); short-circuit terminal errors that fail identically on every model.
Bound the chain, set per-attempt timeouts, and measure per-tier volume, quality, and fallback rate to tune the router safely.
